# SKELETON — IRREVOCABLE LIFE INSURANCE TRUST (ILIT)
### ⚠️ ATTORNEY REVIEW REQUIRED — EDUCATIONAL SKELETON — NOT FOR EXECUTION ⚠️
**Design core:** the policy is owned by the trust from inception (or gifted in within the § 2035 3-year window discipline), so the death benefit escapes § 2042 estate inclusion while providing estate liquidity. **Insured must hold NO incidents of ownership** — never trustee, never a withdrawal-right holder on their own policy.

---

**TRUST AGREEMENT — [NAME] INSURANCE TRUST U/A/D [DATE]**

**GRANTOR(S):** [Insured] (per-policy trusts recommended for multi-insured couples — joint-life/second-to-die policy may use one trust; **verify** second-to-die funding mechanics per spouse's estate plan).
**TRUSTEE:** [Corporate/independent trustee — NOT the insured, NOT the insured's spouse, NOT anyone obligated to pay estate taxes (§ 2042(1)(B) incidents-of-ownership trap)].
**BENEFICIARIES:** Grantor's issue, per stirpes (+ Spouse as discretionary beneficiary [DESIGN DECISION — if Spouse is a beneficiary, income may not be applied to premiums on the Spouse's insurable interest without care — § 677(a)(3) grants income applied to *insured's* premiums creates grantor status, which is the desired trigger; spouse-as-beneficiary is generally fine]).

**KEY CLAUSES:**

**1. IRREVOCABLE / NO RETAINED INTEREST** — Irrevocable; Grantor reserves no right to alter; Protector holds replacement power.

### Passage 25.2
**2. GRANTOR-TRUST POWERS (intentional)** — (a) Trustee (a non-adverse party) may apply income/principal to pay premiums on **the Grantor's life** (§ 677(a)(3)); (b) **Substitution power** § 675(4)(C) (swap equivalent-value assets; trustee, not grantor, holds it); (c) borrow without adequate interest/security § 675(2) [optional]. Result: premiums effectively paid with the Grantor's dollars without gift tax on the income-tax outlay.

**3. POLICY OWNERSHIP & FUNDING**
- Trust is **applicant, owner, and beneficiary** of policy(ies) on Grantor's life: [insurer; policy nos. — PLACEHOLDER].
- Premium funding: annual gifts ($19,000 exclusion-tier × beneficiaries, 2026 — verified; Crummey-funded) → Trustee pays insurer directly.
- **Existing policy transfer:** must occur **3+ years before death** (§ 2035 pullback) or expect inclusion; gift of an existing policy to the insured's ILIT is **excepted from transfer-for-value** as a gift carryover-basis transfer (IRC § 101(a)(2)(C)) — confirm with tax counsel; 7122? no — file Form 712 at transfer; no § 698? — skip.

**4. CRUMMEY WITHDRAWAL** — 5-and-5 (§ 2514(c)); notices to all beneficiaries (guardians for minors); log; unexercised rights lapse; no beneficiary holds withdrawal right on *their own* insured life [if individual policies].

### Passage 25.3
**5. TRUSTEE POWERS** — Pay premiums; borrow against policy (premium financing note terms: [PLACEHOLDER]); hold other assets; **estate-liquidity mechanics**: Trustee may (a) lend to Grantor's estate, (b) purchase assets from the estate, (c) redeem stock to fund redemption obligations [buy-sell coordination — PLACEHOLDER].

**6. DISTRIBUTIONS** — On death proceeds: hold for Issue per [HEMS/age-tier design — PLACEHOLDER]; no mandatory inclusion of Spouse unless designed (marital ILIT alternative).

**7. SPENDTHRIFT / ANTI-ALIENATION / NO CONTEST** — Standard suite [verify situs enforceability].

**8. SITUS / GOVERNING LAW / MIGRATION** — [DE / SD / NV — verify]; Trustee may change situs with Protector consent.

**9. ADMINISTRATION** — Trustee obtains EIN (grantor trust — income on Grantor's 1040; no 1041); annual: premium calendar, Crummey notices, 709 exclusions, policy service review, [illustration monitoring — fiduciary prudence (UPIA)].

**10. TERMINATION** — [At youngest issue's age __ / continue in further trusts — PLACEHOLDER].

## [26] SPCU Trust Skeleton #5: Spousal Lifetime Access Trust (SLAT) Non-Reciprocal Architecture (3 Passages)

### Passage 26.1
# SKELETON — RECIPROCAL SLAT PAIR (SPOUSAL LIFETIME ACCESS TRUSTS)
### ⚠️ ATTORNEY REVIEW REQUIRED — EDUCATIONAL SKELETON — NOT FOR EXECUTION ⚠️
**2026 exemption context (verified Nov. 18, 2026):** $15,000,000 per person; $19,000 annual exclusion. Married couple can move up to $30M gift-tax-free with SLATs. Each spouse retains *indirect* access through the other's trust. **Ethics note: separate counsel for each spouse is mandatory practice — these are two instruments, not one.**

---

## TRUST A — HUSBAND AS GRANTOR (SKELETON)

**TRUST AGREEMENT — [NAME] SLAT TRUST A U/A/D [DATE]**

**GRANTOR:** [Husband]. **TRUSTEE:** [Corporate Trustee — NOT Wife, NOT Husband]. **DISTRIBUTION TRUSTEE (for Wife's benefit):** [independent person]. **TRUST PROTECTOR:** [NAME]. **BENEFICIARIES:** (1) **Wife** (discretionary beneficiary for life), (2) Grantor's issue, per stirpes.

**KEY CLAUSES:**

**1. IRREVOCABILITY & NO BENEFICIAL INTEREST OF GRANTOR** — Irrevocable; Grantor is *not* a beneficiary; Grantor reserves no § 2036/§ 2038 interest.

### Passage 26.2
**2. WIFE'S INTEREST — ANTI-INCLUSION DISCIPLINE** — Wife is a discretionary beneficiary only; if Wife ever serves as trustee, her power is limited to an **HEMS ascertainable standard** exercisable only with a non-adverse party (non-general power — § 2041 safe). No general power of appointment in any beneficiary. **Wife's interest terminates on divorce** (divorce-protection clause: alternate beneficiaries = Grantor's issue; consider also: Wife's interest as non-assignable).

**3. CRUMMEY WITHDRAWAL** — 5-and-5 withdrawal rights (IRC § 2514(c)); notice + log discipline (Vol. XVI § 3).

**4. GRANTOR-TRUST TOGGLE** — [Grantor trust powered (§§ 675(4)(C) swap, 677 variants excluding spouse-income trap) / non-grantor]. Coordinate with tax counsel.

**5. DISTRIBUTIONS** — For Wife: **HEMS only**, by DT (not exercisable by Wife); for Issue: broader discretionary standard [health, education, support, *and* comfort/best interests]; spray powers; no distribution to Excluded Persons (creditors, spouses of issue [optional], Claimants).

**6. SPENDTHRIFT & ANTI-ALIENATION** — Full spendthrift; interests non-assignable; anti-duress clause.

**7. TRUSTEE SUCCESSION & PROTECTOR** — Ladder [1st Corporate; 2nd ___; 3rd ___]; Protector may remove/replace, amend for tax law (decanting-compatible), change situs.

**8. SITUS & GOVERNING LAW** — [SD / DE / NV / WY — verify statute]; exclusive jurisdiction in situs courts; migration clause.

### Passage 26.3
**9. TAX CLAUSES** — GST formula allocation on timely 709; estate-tax apportionment; in terrorem [verify situs enforceability].

**10. TERMINATION** — On Wife's death (if issue all grown): continue for issue in further trusts / distribute per age tiers [DESIGN DECISION — PLACEHOLDER].

## TRUST B — WIFE AS GRANTOR (ANTI-RECIPROCITY DISCIPLINE)
Mirror Trust A **with deliberate differences** — the Reciprocal Trust Doctrine (*United States v. Grace*, 395 U.S. 316 (1969)) ignores cross-gifts that are "mutual in every detail." Vary:
1. **Different trustee** (different corporate fiduciary).
2. **Different distribution standard** for Husband (e.g., HEMS + [education-of-grandchildren] vs. HEMS-only).
3. **Different remainder/timing** (Trust B: no age-tier; Trust A: age-tier at [35/40/45] — pick one design).
4. **Different initial funding** ($[X] vs. $[Y] — not equal).
5. **Staggered funding dates** ([date 1] vs. [date 2 + 30 days]).
6. **Different protector** (different institution/individual).

**EXECUTION CHECKLIST (per trust):** separate counsel engagement letters; Form 709 (year 1: both gifts; allocate GST via formula); Crummey notices; funding schedule; solvency review; coordination with ILIT/dynasty layers.

# SKELETON — THIRD-PARTY SPECIAL NEEDS TRUST (SNT)
### ⚠️ ATTORNEY REVIEW REQUIRED — EDUCATIONAL SKELETON — NOT FOR EXECUTION ⚠️
**Design core:** funded by parents/third parties (NOT the beneficiary) → **no Medicaid payback** requirement (contrast first-party (d)(4)(A) trusts, which require payback, or (d)(4)(C) pooled trusts — see § 7). The entire drafting objective: supplement means-tested benefits (SSI/Medicaid) without disqualifying the beneficiary.

---

**TRUST AGREEMENT — [NAME] SPECIAL NEEDS TRUST U/A/D [DATE]**

**GRANTORS:** [Parents/family members] **TRUSTEE:** [professional/corporate trustee — NOT the beneficiary, NOT a sole beneficiary-controlled party]. **STANDBY/SUCCESSOR TRUSTEE:** [ladder]. **TRUST PROTECTOR/CARE ADVOCATE:** [NAME]. **BENEFICIARY:** [NAME], a person with a disability (definition below).

**KEY CLAUSES:**

**1. DEFINITIONS** — "Government Benefits": SSI, Medicaid, Medicaid waiver programs, housing subsidies, and any other needs-based programs. "Disability": [SSA definition / instrument-defined]. "Supplement" — the governing verb of this trust.

### Passage 27.2
**2. SUPPLEMENT-NOT-SUPPLANT PURPOSE CLAUSE (the heart)** — Trustee shall distribute income and principal **only** to supplement, and never to supplant or reduce, Government Benefits; distributions shall be made so as to preserve eligibility; **no distribution of cash to the Beneficiary**; **no payment for items of support otherwise provided by Government Benefits** (in-kind shelter: rent/food/utilities paid directly can reduce SSI — the "in-kind support and maintenance" rules; the Care Advocate coordinates with the benefits plan).

**3. DISTRIBUTION AUTHORITY (what this trust is FOR)** — Trustee may pay **third parties directly** for: supplemental medical/dental/therapies not covered by Medicaid; equipment; home purchase or modifications [held as exempt-asset strategies — coordinate]; transportation/vehicle; travel, recreation, cultural activities; companion/advocate services; insurance premiums; education; legal fees; and quality-of-life enrichment — all subject to Clause 2.

**4. PROHIBITED DISTRIBUTIONS** — No distributions to or for the direct benefit of [other persons who might be duty-support relatives — anti-support-substitution]; no assets to the Beneficiary's estate; **no governmental-agency payback on termination** (third-party trust — remains available only because no government claim attaches; contrast Vol. note § 7).

### Passage 27.3
**5. SPENDTHRIFT & ANTI-ALIENATION** — Beneficiary may not assign, anticipate, pledge, or otherwise alienate; creditors of the Beneficiary (other than statutory claimants) may not reach trust property; **anti-SNAP?** — anti-"transfer-of-asset" coordination clause: Trustee shall not make transfers that create penalty-period disqualification without written benefits-counsel sign-off.

**6. TRUSTEE POWERS & ADMINISTRATION** — Full investment powers (UPIA); separate books; annual accounting to Protector/family (§ 813(b) discipline); **benefits-eligibility reviews** [annual, with counsel]; letter-of-intent maintenance (care preferences — Exhibit B); 1041 filings; no 3520 (domestic trust).

**7. FIRST-PARTY COMPARISON NOTE (drafting integrity check)** — If ANY asset of the disabled person funds this trust: STOP — that is a first-party trust requiring (a) payback-to-state clause per 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(A), (b) under-65 funding, or a (d)(4)(C) pooled-trust account, drafted to statute — do not use this third-party skeleton.

**8. TRUSTEE SUCCESSION / CARE CONTINUITY** — Ladder of successor trustees; Care Advocate succession; standby guardianship coordination; trust remains until Beneficiary's death, then remainder to [other children/issue — DESIGN DECISION].

**9. GOVERNING LAW / SITUS** — [Family's state — verify state SNT statutes and 1396p conforming amendments]; probate-court reporting where state-required.

### Passage 27.4

### ⚠️ ATTORNEY REVIEW REQUIRED — EDUCATIONAL SKELETON — NOT FOR EXECUTION ⚠️
**§ 664 core requirements (BINDING):** payout ≥ 5% of trust value; charitable remainderman must receive ≥ 10% of initial value (actuarial); CRAT probability-of-exhaustion ≤ 20%. Deduction percentages (AGI tiers) are rate-law-dependent — T-3 verifies current figures at drafting.

---

## INSTRUMENT 1 — CHARITABLE REMAINDER TRUST (CRAT or CRUT)

**GRANTOR(S):** [NAME(S)]. **TRUSTEE:** [individual/corporate]. **CHARITABLE REMAINDERMAN(S):** [§ 170(c) organizations — 501(c)(3) public charities only; **no private foundations** unless 35%-test satisfied].

**1. PAYOUT DESIGN**
- **CRAT:** fixed dollar annuity [__]% of initial funding (5% minimum; verify 7520-based deduction); probability-of-exhaustion test compliance.
- **CRUT:** fixed [__]% of annually-revalued trust value [net-income with make-up (NIMCRUT) variant for cash-flow-poor assets].
- Test actuarial 10% remainder at funding (exhibit: actuary letter).

**2. FUNDING & THE CAPITAL-GAINS WIN** — Appreciated securities/real estate contributed **in kind**; CRT sells tax-free (§ 664(c) exemption) and reinvests — grantor bypasses embedded gain; income taxed to grantor/beneficiaries under the 4-tier § 664 ordering (ordinary → capital gain → other → principal).

### Passage 28.2
**3. CLAUSES** — Irrevocable; no grantor-trust status (must be non-grantor to qualify); trustee powers limited (prudent investor; no self-dealing beyond § 664(d)(2)(B) narrow sale rules); annual Form 5227; Form 1041-R? — CRT files 1041 with § 664 characterizations; deduction substantiation (Form 8283; qualified appraisal for >$5,000 — verify current threshold).

**4. TERMINATION** — On expiration: remainder to charity(ies) per formula [fixed shares].

## INSTRUMENT 2 — CHARITABLE LEAD TRUST (CLAT)

**1. DESIGN CHOICE** — **Grantor CLAT:** immediate income-tax deduction of the annuity's present value; grantor taxed on trust income (pairs with sale strategies). **Non-grantor CLAT:** estate-tax deduction at death; requires **≥ 10% charitable remainder** for the estate deduction.
- **Zeroed-out CLAT** (*Estate of Walton v. Commissioner*, 274 F.3d 881 (5th Cir. 2001)): annuity to charity = full initial value at the § 7520 rate → remainder to family with **zero gift value**; downside if assets underperform the rate (mirror of GRAT logic, reversed).

**2. SKELETON CLAUSES** — Term: [10–20] years; charitable annuity: $[____]/yr to [§ 170(c) charities, fixed shares]; rest to family in further trust at term end; grantor-trust toggle [§ 674 grantor CLAT for deduction]; GST allocation for remainder [formula on 709]; yearly Form 5227; annuity payment calendar (Missed annuity = trust-failure risk — D&O the calendar).

### Passage 28.3
## INSTRUMENT 3 — DONOR-ADVISED FUND (DAF) (comparison note)
No instrument needed — account at a sponsoring organization: immediate deduction (AGI tiers: cash up to 60%? — verify current tiers), no distributions floor (vs. private foundation's 5% payout and excise tax — verify current rate), least control. Use DAF for flexibility; CRT for income; CLAT for estate-tax offset; **private foundation** only when family control of grants is essential (1.39%-band excise — verify; self-dealing/excess-holdings rules are strict).

**CHARITABLE-LAYER DECISION TABLE (swarm T-1 uses this):**
| Client need | Instrument |
|---|---|
| Income now + diversify appreciated asset tax-free | CRUT/CRAT |
| Estate-tax deduction + family remainder upside | Zeroed-out CLAT |
| Simplicity + ongoing giving flexibility | DAF |
| Family grant-making control | Private foundation (accept compliance burden) |

# SKELETON — FREEZE INSTRUMENTS (GRAT + IDGT INSTALLMENT SALE)
### ⚠️ ATTORNEY REVIEW REQUIRED — EDUCATIONAL SKELETON — NOT FOR EXECUTION ⚠️
**Rates rule:** every GRAT annuity and IDGT note is priced off the **current-month § 7520 rate / current AFR** — the swarm's T-3 agent must pull the live rate (IRS.lv monthly tables) at drafting. **Verified 2026 context:** $15M exemption, $19k exclusion (Nov. 18, 2026).

---

## INSTRUMENT 1 — ZEROED-OUT GRAT (Walton GRAT)

**GRANTOR:** [NAME]. **TRUSTEE:** [independent/institutional — grantor-trust powered]. **REMAINDER BENEFICIARIES:** [Dynasty Trust / children — often "to a continuing dynasty trust" so no gift of remainder].

**1. TERM** — [2–10] years, ending [last day of month — GRATs must end at month-end]. **Ladder strategy:** fund [3–5] GRATs of staggered terms [2/5/10 yr] for rate diversification. Grantor must **survive the term** (death within term → inclusion under § 2036; consider short-term GRAT + life-insurance hedge pairing).

### Passage 30.2
**2. ANNUITY (the zero-out engine)** — Annual annuity to Grantor computed under the **Walton formula** (*Walton v. Commissioner*, 115 S. Ct. 2026 (1995)): amounts equal to the initial funding's value rebated at the § 7520 rate, so the actuarial value of the remainder ≈ **$0** → gift value ≈ $0 → **no exemption consumed**. Annuity payable [annually; April 30 deadline mechanics per Rev. Proc. practice — verify current revenue procedure for late-payment recharacterization].

**3. FUNDING** — Volatile, high-growth assets only (concentrated stock, LLC interests — appraised): $[____]. Underperforming assets waste the GRAT (annuity returns capital) — the downside is opportunity cost, not loss.

**4. GRANTOR-TRUST POWERS** — § 675(4)(C) substitution + other 672–677-compatible powers (income tax to grantor; trust inside-out growth compounds to remainder).

**5. GST PAIRING** — Remainder to GST-exempt dynasty trust; formula GST allocation if exemption available (T-3 verifies ceiling).

**6. MECHANICAL CLAUSES** — No commingling of GRAT assets; separate books per GRAT (rolling strategy); trustee may satisfy annuity in-kind [in cash or in-kind per current revenue-procedure rules]; prohibition on grantor serving as sole trustee.

## INSTRUMENT 2 — IDGT INSTALLMENT SALE

**SELLER/GRANTOR:** [NAME]. **BUYER TRUST:** irrevocable grantor trust for [Issue — Grantor NOT beneficiary].

### Passage 30.3
**1. SEED CAPITAL (bonding requirement)** — Gift of **≥ 10% of contemplated purchase price** to the trust before the sale (cushion against the *Estate of* harmony? — against note being recharacterized as prearranged/§ 2036 transaction; the widely-used 10% bonding practice — confirm with tax counsel).

**2. THE SALE** — Trust purchases assets (appraised: $[____]) for a **full-recourse-installment note** at the **long-term AFR** (current month — T-3 pulls live rate), interest-only or amortizing; term [5–20 yr]; balloon at maturity.

**3. WHY IT FREEZES** — Growth above the AFR compounds **inside the trust, outside the estate, gift-tax-free**; the note is a non-event for estate tax (§ 2036/§ 2038 discipline: no retained enjoyment/control); **grantor-trust status means the grantor's own income tax on trust income is not a gift** (Rev. Rul. 85-13 line; Rev. Rul. 2004-64 for payments) — the "extra gift" engine.

**4. GUARANTEE DISCIPLINE** — Grantor must **not personally guarantee** the note (guarantee invites § 2036 inclusion/income recognition; note the internal "no-recourse" structuring).

**5. NOTE-ADMINISTRATION CLAUSES** — Interest paid annually at AFR (validate with market-rate memo — § 7872 discipline); Trustee may refinance; **swap power** (§ 675(4)(C)) lets the grantor substitute low-basis assets at death for basis step-up — coordinate with T-3.

### Passage 30.4
**6. ESTATE-INCLUSION GUARDRAILS** — No management obligations by grantor post-sale (or compensated at FMV via management agreement); formalities: board minutes, invoices, bank ledger of payments.

**7. VARIANTS** — **SCIN** (self-canceling note) where grantor's life expectancy is short (premium priced by actuarial tables); **sale to SLAT/dynasty** combinations (which trust is the buyer is a design decision with the SLAT's access tradeoff).

**EXECUTION CHECKLIST:** independent trustee in place → seed gift documented (709) → appraisal (Schedule A) → note executed at current AFR (live rate certified in file) → funding assignment → annual interest ledger → 709/gift log → swap-power memo on file.

## [32] SPCU Volume I: Foundations and Types of Sovereignty (14 Passages)

### Passage 32.1
# VOLUME I — FOUNDATIONS AND TYPES OF SOVEREIGNTY

## 1. Executive Overview

Sovereignty is the suprema potestas — supreme authority within a territory — and United States law distributes it across **four interacting layers**: the people (popular sovereignty), the national government (external and delegated sovereignty), the states (residual internal sovereignty), and the tribes (retained inherent sovereignty). Foreign states, diplomats, and territories hold distinct, statutorily and constitutionally defined immunities. Every modern U.S. doctrine of sovereignty is *institutional* — it attaches to governments, nations, and tribes — and no court has ever recognized a category of *personal* sovereignty that exempts an individual from generally applicable law. Theories of "individual sovereignty" advanced in court are rejected, and are separately classified in Volume VIII.

## 2. Detailed Legal Explanation — Each Doctrine

### Passage 32.2
### 2.1 Popular sovereignty
**Doctrine.** The people are the ultimate source of governmental authority; governments "deriv[e] their just powers from the consent of the governed." Declaration of Independence (1776). Madison, Federalist No. 49: "the people are the only legitimate fountain of power." The Constitution was ordained by "We the People" and ratified by special conventions (Art. VII), not by the state legislatures — the structural point of *McCulloch v. Maryland*, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819): the federal government "emanates from the people" and "its powers are assuredly granted" by them, not by the states.
**Status:** BINDING (constitutional structure).

### 2.2 National sovereignty (external)
**Doctrine.** The United States, as a nation, holds inherent external sovereignty — the power to conduct foreign affairs, wage war, admit and exclude aliens, and govern territory — not because the states delegated it but because nationhood carries it. *United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.*, 299 U.S. 304 (1936) (Sutherland, J.): the federal government's external powers "are the resultant of ... thepower to declare and wage war ... and to effectuate it through diplomatic channels."
**Status:** BINDING.

### Passage 32.3
### 2.3 State sovereignty and the Eleventh Amendment
**Doctrine.** States entered the Union with "residual sovereignty" over all else. But state sovereign immunity from federal suits is a constitutional rule: ratified in reaction to *Chisholm v. Georgia*, 2 U.S. (2 Dall.) 419 (1793) (suit against a state by a South Carolina creditor allowed), the Eleventh Amendment (1795) bars federal-jurisdiction suits by a citizen against his own state, and *Hans v. Louisiana*, 134 U.S. 1 (1890), extended the bar to federal-question claims. The modern line:
- *Seminole Tribe of Fla. v. Florida*, 517 U.S. 44 (1996) — Congress may not abrogate state immunity under its Article I (Indian Commerce) powers.
- *Alden v. Maine*, 527 U.S. 706 (1999) — immunity also bars state-court suits against states; sovereign immunity "derives from" the constitutional structure.
**Exceptions (all BINDING):** (1) state consent (*Lapides v. Bd. of Regents*, 535 U.S. 613 (2002) — removing from state to federal court waives immunity); (2) Congress may abrogate under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment (*Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer*, 427 U.S. 445 (1976); *Nev. Dep't of Human Res. v. Hibbs*, 538 U.S. 721 (2003)); (3) *Ex parte Young*, 209 U.S. 123 (1908) — prospective relief against a state officer for ongoing violations of federal law is not a suit against the state.
**Status:** BINDING.

### Passage 32.4
### 2.4 Internal vs. external sovereignty
Internal sovereignty = authority over domestic affairs, distributed by federalism (see Volume II). External sovereignty = nationhood capacity, lodged exclusively in the federal government. States cannot conduct foreign policy, coin money, or enter treaties (Art. I § 10).

### 2.5 Territorial sovereignty
**Doctrine.** Congress governs territories under Art. IV § 3 cl. 2 with "plenary" power, but constitutional guarantees follow (*Downes v. Bidwell*, 182 U.S. 244 (1901), and the Insular Cases). *Puerto Rico v. Sánchez Valle*, 579 U.S. 59 (2016): Puerto Rico is not a separate sovereign for double-jeopardy purposes — sovereignty over Puerto Rico traces to Congress. *United States v. Vaello Madero*, 596 U.S. 286 (2022): Congress may exclude Puerto Rico residents from Supplemental Security Income without violating equal protection.
**Status:** BINDING (the Insular Cases' framework is criticized by scholars; unresolved: their future).

### Passage 32.5
### 2.6 Indigenous and tribal sovereignty
**Doctrine.** Tribes retain inherent sovereignty as "distinct, independent political communities" predating the Constitution. Key authorities:
- *Johnson v. M'Intosh*, 21 U.S. (8 Wheat.) 543 (1823) — discovery doctrine; tribes hold aboriginal title subject to the discoverer's extinguishment power.
- *Worcester v. Georgia*, 31 U.S. (6 Pet.) 515 (1832) — tribes are "distinct political communities, having territorial boundaries, within which their authority is exclusive."
- *United States v. Wheeler*, 435 U.S. 313 (1978) — tribal sovereignty is *retained*, not *delegated*; tribal prosecution is not a second "separate sovereign" prosecution (no double jeopardy bar).
- *Duro v. Reina*, 495 U.S. 676 (1990) — tribes lack criminal jurisdiction over nonmember Indians; *United States v. Lara*, 541 U.S. 193 (2004) — Congress may constitutionally restore it (Duro-fix legislation).
- *Montana v. United States*, 450 U.S. 544 (1981) — tribes generally lack civil regulatory authority over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land, subject to the "Montana exceptions."
- *McGirt v. Oklahoma*, 590 U.S. 250 (2020) — the Muscogee (Creek) Reservation was never disestablished; state criminal courts lacked jurisdiction over crimes by Indians on it.
- *Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta*, 597 U.S. 629 (2022) — states have concurrent jurisdiction over crimes by non-Indians against Indians on Indian land absent federal preemptio

### Passage 32.6
s on it.
- *Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta*, 597 U.S. 629 (2022) — states have concurrent jurisdiction over crimes by non-Indians against Indians on Indian land absent federal preemption.
- *Haaland v. Brackeen*, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — the Indian Child Welfare Act is constitutional; Congress's Indian-affairs power is broad.
- Tribal sovereign immunity from suit: *Kiowa Tribe v. Mfg. Tech., Inc.*, 523 U.S. 751 (1998).
**Status:** BINDING, and currently evolving (state/tribal jurisdiction litigation continues into the 2025–26 term).

### Passage 32.7
### 2.7 Diplomatic immunity
Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961), arts. 22–31: full immunity for diplomatic agents from criminal jurisdiction, qualified immunity civilly; inviolability of premises. Implemented in U.S. law (22 U.S.C. §§ 254a–254d). Status: BINDING (ratified treaty + statute).

### 2.8 Foreign sovereign immunity
**Doctrine.** From absolute immunity (*The Schooner Exchange v. McFaddon*, 11 U.S. (7 Cranch) 116 (1812)) to the restrictive theory (U.S. Dept. of State "Tate Letter," 1952), codified in the **Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976**, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 — the exclusive basis for suit (Argentina v. Amerada Hess, 488 U.S. 428 (1989)). Core exceptions: waiver; commercial activity (*Republic of Argentina v. Weltover*, 504 U.S. 607 (1992)); expropriation "in violation of international law" — *German v. Philipp*, 592 U.S. 118 (2021) (genocide exception reaches only genocide, and requires taking property in violation of the law of nations); *Hungary v. Simon*, 590 U.S. 30 (2020). *Republic of Austria v. Altmann*, 541 U.S. 677 (2004) — FSIA applies retroactively.
**Status:** BINDING.

### Passage 32.8
### 2.9 Sovereign immunity of the United States
The United States is immune from suit without express statutory consent, strictly construed (*Lane v. Peña*, 518 U.S. 187 (1996)); principal waivers: Federal Tort Claims Act (28 U.S.C. § 1346(b)); Tucker Act (28 U.S.C. § 1491); Little Tucker Act; Bankruptcy Code § 106. Status: BINDING.

### 2.10 Sovereign equality of states
UN Charter art. 2(1) ("Sovereign equality of all its Members"); *Island of Palmas* (Neth. v. U.S.), 2 R.I.I.A. 829 (Perm. Ct. Arb. 1928) (Huber, arb.): sovereignty is "the right to exercise ... the functions of a State to the exclusion of any other State." Equal states, unequal power — equality is a *legal* rule.

### Passage 32.9
### 2.11 Self-determination
UN Charter art. 1(2); ICCPR art. 1 ("All peoples have the right of self-determination"). Legally operative forms: decolonization, internal self-government. Secession has no general right in international law: *Reference re Secession of Quebec*, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 217 (Can.); *Accordance with International Law of the Unilateral Declaration of Independence of Kosovo*, Advisory Opinion, 2010 I.C.J. 141 (declaration did not violate international law, but the Court declined to say international law confers a right to secede). Domestically: *Texas v. White*, 74 U.S. (7 Wall.) 700 (1869) — the Union is "indissoluble"; there is no state right of unilateral secession.
**Status:** BINDING/BEST-READ — and the decisive answer to "sovereign exits" theories (Volume VIII).

### 2.12 De facto vs. de jure sovereignty
A recognition-law distinction (Lauterpacht, *Recognition in International Law* (1947)): de jure recognition is the legal acknowledgment of statehood/government; de facto recognition is provisional acknowledgment of effective control. Status: PERSUASIVE (customary practice).

### Passage 32.10
### 2.13 Parliamentary / constitutional sovereignty (comparative)
United Kingdom: Parliament is the supreme lawmaking body (A.V. Dicey, *Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution* (1885)); in the U.S., "constitutional sovereignty" — the Constitution itself is supreme (Art. VI; *Cooper v. Aaron*, 358 U.S. 1 (1958): "the federal judiciary is supreme in the exposition of the law of the Constitution"). Detailed treatment: Volume XI.

### 2.14 Federalism and reserved powers
Tenth Amendment: powers not delegated nor prohibited are "reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." Anti-commandeering: *Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Ass'n*, 584 U.S. 363 (2018) — Congress may not compel state officers to execute federal law, but states may not nullify federal law either.

### Passage 32.11
### 2.15 Citizenship, nationality, domicile, residency
Status concepts (full treatment: Volume V): **citizenship** (8 U.S.C. § 1401 — birth in the U.S.; § 1431 et seq. — derivation; § 1421 — naturalization), **nationality** (includes noncitizen nationals of American Samoa), **domicile** (the one place of true, fixed, permanent home — Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §§ 11–23), **residence** (mere physical presence, legally weaker than domicile). None of these statuses exempts a person from generally applicable law; claiming otherwise was rejected in *Meads v. Meads*, 848 F.2d 66 (9th Cir. 1988), and *United States v. Benabe*, 633 F.3d 581 (7th Cir. 2011).

### Passage 32.12
### 2.16 Historical "individual sovereignty" theories — judicial treatment
Founding-era usage: Wilson and Iredell, concurring in *Chisholm*, described "sovereignty of the people" in rhetorically individualist terms; Blackstone described "absolute rights" of persons. Modern courts read none of this as personal exemption from law. Controlling rejection: *Meads v. Meads*, 848 F.2d 66, 68–69 (9th Cir. 1988) (cataloguing "individual sovereignty," "freemen," "Posse Comitatus," and related arguments as without foundation); *United States v. Benabe*, 633 F.3d 581, 587 (7th Cir. 2011) ("Regardless of an individual's claimed status of descent, be it as a 'sovereign citizen,' a 'secured-party creditor,' or a 'flesh-and-blood human being' ... that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts."); the Seventh Circuit has called "sovereign-citizen immunity" defenses "frivolous" (see *United States v. Willis*, 8th Cir. 2024, collecting). **Status: REJECTED.** Full dossier: Volume VIII.

### Passage 32.13
## 3. Historical Foundations
Sovereignty theory: Jean Bodin, *Six Books of the Commonwealth* (1576) (indivisible supreme power); Hobbes, *Leviathan* (1651); Emer de Vattel, *The Law of Nations* (1758) (states as moral persons). The American innovation: sovereignty split between a national government of enumerated powers and states of reserved powers, grounded in the people — the architecture *McCulloch* and *Gibbons v. Ogden*, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) 1 (1824), map.

## 4. Practical Legal Applications
- Choosing the defendant controls Eleventh Amendment exposure (state vs. officer; prospective vs. retrospective relief).
- Tribal jurisdiction analysis runs through the Montana framework (civil) and McGirt/Castro-Huerta (criminal).
- FSIA is a mandatory screen — service under § 1608 and exhaustion; a missed FSIA argument forfeits nothing else but dooms the case.
- Status questions (citizenship, domicile, nationality) are governed by statute and treaty — not by declaration or paperwork choices.

## 5. Unresolved Questions
- The future of the Insular Cases (called into question but not overruled; *Vaello Madero* declined to revisit them).
- The outer bounds of tribal civil jurisdiction over nonmembers after *Castro-Huerta*.
- Scope of § 5 abrogation after *Collins v. Yellen*, 594 U.S. 220 (2021), narrowing *Fitzpatrick* for claims against agencies' officers.

### Passage 32.14
## 6. Source Notes
All cases cited by U.S. Reports / S. Ct. citations; treaty sources: UN Charter; VCDR (1961); ICCPR (1966); Montevideo Convention (1933). Verified against live research this session; access date November 18, 2026.

## [33] SPCU Volume II: Constitutional Authority & Government Structure (7 Passages)

### Passage 33.1
# VOLUME II — CONSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY AND GOVERNMENT STRUCTURE

## 1. Executive Overview
Federal authority rests on **enumeration** (Art. I § 8), **supremacy** (Art. VI), and **separation of powers** (the tripartite structure). Judicial review (*Marbury v. Madison*, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803)) makes the courts the expositors of that authority — a role reinforced in *Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo* (U.S. June 28, 2024), which overruled *Chevron* deference and directed that **courts, not agencies, decide questions of law**. As of November 18, 2026, the governing separation-of-powers landscape includes *SEC v. Jarkesy* (June 27, 2024) and *FCC v. Consumers' Research* (June 27, 2025).

### Passage 33.2
## 2. Enumerated Powers
- **Necessary and Proper Clause**, Art. I § 8 cl. 18: *McCulloch v. Maryland*, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819) — Congress may choose any rationally related means to execute enumerated powers; states may not impede federal instrumentalities.
- **Commerce Clause**, Art. I § 8 cl. 3: *Gibbons v. Ogden*, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) 1 (1824); outer expansion *Wickard v. Filburn*, 317 U.S. 111 (1942); modern limits *United States v. Lopez*, 514 U.S. 549 (1995) (noneconomic gun possession), *United States v. Morrison*, 529 U.S. 598 (2000) (VAWA civil remedy), *NFIB v. Sebelius*, 567 U.S. 519 (2012) (Medicaid coercion).
- **Taxing/Spending:** Art. I § 8 cl. 1; *Biden v. Nebraska*, 600 U.S. 477 (2023) (major-questions approach to spending power).

## 3. Supremacy and Judicial Review
Art. VI cl. 2. *Martin v. Hunter's Lessee*, 14 U.S. (1 Wheat.) 304 (1816) (federal appellate power over state courts on federal questions). *Cooper v. Aaron*, 358 U.S. 1 (1958): "the federal judiciary is supreme in the exposition of the law of the Constitution" — every state and federal officer is bound. There is no procedure by which a private "declaration" or filing removes a person from this structure.

### Passage 33.3
## 4. Separation of Powers — Current Law (verified to Nov. 18, 2026)
| Decision | Date | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| *Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer*, 343 U.S. 579 (1952) | 1952 | Presidential action must trace to Congress or the Constitution; Justice Jackson's tripartite framework |
| *Clinton v. City of New York*, 524 U.S. 417 (1998) | 1998 | Line-item veto violates bicameralism/presentment |
| *Seila Law LLC v. CFPB*, 591 U.S. 197 (2020); *Collins v. Yellen*, 594 U.S. 220 (2021) | 2020–21 | Limits on for-cause removal protection for single directors |
| **SEC v. Jarkesy**, 603 U.S. 109 (2024) (No. 22-859, decided June 27, 2024) | 2024 | When the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud mirroring common-law fraud, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial in federal court — the "public rights" exception does not reach it |
| **Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo**, 603 U.S. 369 (2024) (No. 22-451, decided June 28, 2024) | 2024 | **Chevron deference overruled**; courts must independently decide statutory meaning (prior reliance-based holdings survive) |
| **FCC v. Consumers' Research**, 605 U.S. ___ (2025) (No. 24-354, decided June 27, 2025) | 2025 | The universal-service contribution scheme does **not** violate the nondelegation doctrine; Congress provided sufficient guiding principles; no heightened standard for revenue-raising delegations |

### Passage 33.4
**Nondelegation doctrine today:** the intelligible-principle test of *J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States*, 279 U.S. 481 (1929), remains the operative rule; *Gundy v. United States*, 139 S. Ct. 2116 (2019), preserved it; *West Virginia v. EPA*, 597 U.S. 697 (2022), and *Biden v. Nebraska* added the "major questions" clear-statement approach; *Consumers' Research* (2025) confirmed delegation survives in the revenue context. The doctrine constrains agencies — it has never been a vehicle to challenge the validity of the federal government itself.

## 5. Incorporation of the Bill of Rights
*Barron v. Baltimore*, 32 U.S. (7 Pet.) 243 (1833) (no incorporation against states pre-1868) → through the Fourteenth Amendment: *Gitlow v. New York*, 268 U.S. 652 (1925); *Duncan v. Louisiana*, 391 U.S. 145 (1968); *McDonald v. Chicago*, 561 U.S. 742 (2010); *Timbs v. Indiana*, 586 U.S. 146 (2019) (excessive fines). Nearly the entire Bill of Rights now binds the states — relevant because "state citizen" theories assume the opposite.

### Passage 33.5
## 6. Territorial Government and the District of Columbia
- **Territories:** *American Insurance Co. v. Canter*, 26 U.S. (1 Pet.) 511 (1828) — Congress may create territorial (Article IV) courts; *Downes v. Bidwell*, 182 U.S. 244 (1901) (Insular Cases).
- **D.C.:** Article I § 8 cl. 17 gives Congress "exclusive Legislation" over the seat of government. The **Organic Act of 1871** created a territorial-style government for the District; it was replaced in 1874 and superseded by a commissioner government (1878); the **Home Rule Act of 1973**, Pub. L. 93-198, created the current elected government. *Palmore v. United States*, 411 U.S. 389 (1973) — D.C. local courts are valid Article I courts. **Nothing in any of these acts converted the United States into a corporation** (Volume VII dissects the 28 U.S.C. § 3002(15) definition that fuels this claim).

### Passage 33.6
## 7. Emergency Powers and Martial Law
- Statutory architecture: Trading with the Enemy Act (1917); **National Emergencies Act (1976)** — terminated all then-existing emergencies and created the declaration/termination regime; IEEPA (1977).
- Constitutional limits: *Ex parte Milligan*, 71 U.S. (4 Wall.) 2 (1866) — no military trial of civilians where civil courts are open; *Duncan v. Kahanamoku*, 327 U.S. 304 (1946); *Youngstown* (1952). *Trump v. Hawaii*, 138 S. Ct. 2392 (2018) formally repudiated *Korematsu*.
- **Conclusion (BINDING):** No declared emergency suspends the Constitution or the civilian courts. "The emergency is still on" is not a legal argument; it has been rejected wherever asserted (Volume VIII).

## 8. Practical Applications
- A party challenging federal action must attack the *specific* statute's delegation or application — *Loper Bright* makes statutory-text arguments more powerful in court than they have been since 1984; *Jarkesy* restores jury rights in common-law-like penalty actions.
- None of this creates a "private law" channel, a "de facto" court, or a consent-based exemption. The lawful paths are the ordinary ones: motions, appeals, constitutional litigation.

### Passage 33.7
## 9. Unresolved Questions
- The reach of *Jarkesy* beyond SEC fraud penalties (RESERVE-focused agencies; FTC; FINRA) remains contested in the circuits.
- "Major questions" doctrine's outer boundaries.
- Removal-power litigation in the 2025–26 term (*Trump v. Slaughter* line) — watch for updates.

Official slip opinions verified this session: [SEC v. Jarkesy (June 27, 2024)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/22-859_1924.pdf); [Loper Bright (June 28, 2024)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/22-451_7m58.pdf); [FCC v. Consumers' Research (June 27, 2025)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/24pdf/24-354_0861.pdf). Accessed November 18, 2026.

## [34] SPCU Volume III: Admiralty & Maritime Law Jurisdiction (10 Passages)

### Passage 34.1
# VOLUME III — COMPLETE ADMIRALTY AND MARITIME LAW

## 1. Executive Overview
Admiralty law is a **specialized federal subject-matter jurisdiction** governing maritime commerce, torts on navigable waters, seamen, vessels, and salvage. It exists alongside — not instead of — ordinary civil jurisdiction. The claims that admiralty law secretly governs every citizen, courtroom, or birth certificate are pseudolegal inventions rejected by controlling courts (Section 10 below and Volume VIII).

## 2. Historical Foundations
| Era | Source | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Antiquity | **Rhodian Sea Law** (customs of Rhodes, compiled in the Byzantine *Nomos Rhodion Nautikos*) | Earliest systematic maritime customs (jettison, collision) |
| ~1150–1190 | **Rolls of Oléron** (Atlantic/La Rochelle; English usage attributed to Eleanor of Aquitaine's era) | Judgment-based code for masters, crews, merchants |
| ~13th–15th c. | **Laws of Wisby**; Hanseatic codes | Baltic commercial law |
| ~14th c. | **Consolato del Mare** (Barcelona) | Comprehensive Mediterranean code |
| 14th–19th c. | **English High Court of Admiralty**; *Black Book of the Admiralty* | Instance and prize jurisdiction; constant friction with common-law courts |
| 1758–1805 | Vattel; Blackstone | The treatise vocabulary the Framers absorbed |

### Passage 34.2
Colonial America used vice-admiralty courts (notably for Navigation Acts enforcement — a grievance in the Declaration of Independence). After 1776, the Articles of Confederation left admiralty largely to the states — one of the failures that motivated the Constitution.

## 3. Constitutional and Statutory Basis
- **Article III, § 2:** judicial power extends to "all Cases of admiralty and maritime Jurisdiction."
- **Judiciary Act of 1789, § 9:** district-court cognizance, *exclusive* over civil admiralty causes — "saving to suitors, in all cases, the right of a common law remedy where the common law is competent to give it." Codified today at **28 U.S.C. § 1333**.
- *De Lovio v. Boit*, 7 F. Cas. 418 (C.C.D. Mass. 1815) (Story, J.) — the founding-era defense of full federal admiralty jurisdiction; *The Genesee Chief*, 53 U.S. (12 How.) 443 (1851) — admiralty extends to the Great Lakes and all navigable waters, overruling the tidal-waters limit of *The Thomas Jefferson*, 10 U.S. (10 Wheat.) 428 (1825).
- **Procedure:** Supplemental Rules for Certain Admiralty and Maritime Claims (Rules B–G) — attachment (B), suits in rem (C, D), vessel arrest/forfeiture (G).

### Passage 34.3
## 4. Jurisdiction Tests (BINDING)
1. **Tort (maritime but non-vessel):** *Executive Jet Aviation v. City of Cleveland*, 418 U.S. 669 (1974) — locality **plus** "a significant relationship to traditional maritime activity"; refined in *Sisson v. Diamond*, 496 U.S. 708 (1990), and *Jerome B. Grubart, Inc. v. Great Lakes Dredge & Dock Co.*, 513 U.S. 527 (1995) (location + connection test). *Foremost Insurance Co. v. Richardson*, 457 U.S. 668 (1982) — collisions between commercial vessels are covered even off navigable waters.
2. **"Vessel":** *Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach*, 568 U.S. 115 (2013) — "a reasonable observer, looking to the home's physical characteristics and activities" test; *Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach (II)*, 585 U.S. 87 (2018) — maritime lien requires "some realistic connection to ... maritime activity."
3. **Contract:** *Kossick v. United Fruit*, 365 U.S. 731 (1961); *Norfolk Southern R.R. v. James N. Kirby, Sons*, 543 U.S. 14 (2004) — bills of lading' incorporation of arbitration clauses governs intermodal carriers.
4. **Navigable waters:** *The Daniel Ball*, 77 U.S. (10 Wall.) 557 (1871) ("navigable waters of the United States"); *The Robert W. Parsons*, 191 U.S. 17 (1903) (capable of use for interstate/foreign commerce).

### Passage 34.4
## 5. Core Doctrines and Remedies
- **General maritime law** is "a body of law" courts apply as part of the federal judicial power (*Southern Pacific Co. v. Jensen*, 244 U.S. 205 (1917)); it yields to contrary federal statute (*Miles v. Apex Marine Corp.*, 498 U.S. 19 (1990)) and yields to state law in gaps absent conflict (*Yamaha Motor Corp. v. Calhoun*, 516 U.S. 199 (1996)).
- **Maritime liens:** in rem enforceable liens arising by operation of law (*The Blaze Star*, 127 U.S. 84 (1888)); exclusive in rem jurisdiction (*The Plymouth*, 70 U.S. (3 Wall.) 20 (1865)).
- **Salvage & general average:** *Columbus-America Discovery Group v. Atlantic Mutual Ins. Co.*, 974 F.2d 450 (4th Cir. 1992); *Treasure Salvors, Inc. v. Unidentified Wrecked Vessel*, 458 U.S. 670 (1982); York-Antwerp Rules; Abandoned Shipwreck Act, 43 U.S.C. §§ 2101–2106.
- **Carriage of goods:** Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 46 U.S.C. §§ 30701–30707; Harter Act; bills of lading doctrine (*Kirby*, above).
- **Marine insurance:** state law governs absent conflict (*Wilburn Boat Co. v. Fireman's Fund Ins. Co.*, 348 U.S. 310 (1955)).
- **Limitation of Liability Act**, 46 U.S.C. §§ 30501–30511: shipowner may cap liability at vessel value; *Lewis v. Lewis & Clark Marine, Inc.*, 519 U.S. 215 (1997). Recent: *Great Lakes Insurance SE v. Raiders Retreat Realty Co.*, 601 U.S. 659 (U.S. Feb. 21, 2024) — choice-of-law clauses in maritime contracts are presumptively enforceab

### Passage 34.5
1997). Recent: *Great Lakes Insurance SE v. Raiders Retreat Realty Co.*, 601 U.S. 659 (U.S. Feb. 21, 2024) — choice-of-law clauses in maritime contracts are presumptively enforceable absent conflict with federal statute.

### Passage 34.6
## 6. Seamen and Maritime Workers
- **Jones Act** (Merchant Marine Act 1920, § 33; now **46 U.S.C. § 30104**): negligence remedy; seaman status under *Chandris, Inc. v. Latsis*, 515 U.S. 347 (1990) (substantial connection — the "30%" rule).
- **Maintenance and cure**; unseaworthiness; punitive damages available (*Atlantic Sounding Co. v. Townsend*, 557 U.S. 404 (2009)).
- **LHWCA**, 33 U.S.C. § 901 et seq. — administrative compensation for harbor workers; *Southwest Marine, Inc. v. Gizoni*, 502 U.S. 81 (1991) (remedies are mutually exclusive).

### Passage 34.7
## 7. Flag State, Port State, and the Law of the Sea
- **Contacts analysis:** *Lauritzen v. Larsen*, 345 U.S. 571 (1953); *Hellenic Lines Ltd. v. Rhoditis*, 398 U.S. 306 (1970).
- **Prize law:** *The Prize Cases*, 67 U.S. (2 Black) 635 (1863); *Brown v. United States*, 12 U.S. (8 Cranch) 110 (1814).
- **UNCLOS** (opened 1982; in force 1994): **the United States is not a party** — the Senate has never given consent; U.S. practice largely tracks it unilaterally (CRS, IF12578: "The United States is not a party to UNCLOS, but related U.S. law largely comports with its provisions"). Party count is in the mid-160s to low-170s depending on counting date (sources differ; roughly 168 parties reported in 2021 references). U.S. zones: 12-nm territorial sea (Proclamation 5928, 1988), 24-nm contiguous zone (Proclamation 7219, 1999), 200-nm EEZ (Proclamation 5031, 1983).
- International tribunals: ITLOS (Hamburg); ICJ; arbitral annexes.

### Passage 34.8
## 8. The Relationship Between Maritime Law and Ordinary Civil Jurisdiction (BINDING)
The "saving to suitors" clause means a maritime plaintiff may **choose** the federal in rem admiralty action or an ordinary in personam suit at law (state or federal, where jurisdiction lies). *The Plymouth*, 70 U.S. (3 Wall.) 20 (1865): only the in rem remedy is exclusive to admiralty. Therefore: **admiralty is a concurrent forum for many disputes, not a shadow legal system**. Ordinary citizens are governed by ordinary law; admiralty jurisdiction is triggered by maritime facts — not by flags, fonts, or rituals.

### Passage 34.9
## 9. Maritime Pseudolaw — the Claim Set and Its Judicial Status (verified to Nov. 18, 2026)
| Claim | Reality | Status |
|---|---|---|
| "A gold-fringed flag makes a courtroom an admiralty court" | Flag display has zero jurisdictional significance | **REJECTED** — *McCann v. Greenway*, 952 F. Supp. 647 (W.D. Mo. 1997) (theory dismissed as frivolous); repeatedly rejected by other courts; 18 U.S.C. § 7's "special maritime and territorial jurisdiction" is a *criminal-law* venue statute for places (ships, planes, federal enclaves) — it does not govern people |
| "Birth certificates create admiralty/ maritime bonds" | Birth records are state vital-statistics documents; no security exists | **REJECTED/UNSUPPORTED** — TreasuryDirect fraud advisory: "'Birth certificate bonds' do not exist"; see Vol. VII–VIII |
| "Admiralty law governs ordinary citizens because the U.S. is under maritime/military law" | Civilian courts operate continuously under the Constitution | **REJECTED** — *Ex parte Milligan*, 71 U.S. (4 Wall.) 2 (1866) |
| "Naming conventions (capital letters) create maritime persons" | Capitalization is orthography, not law | **REJECTED** — see Volume VIII |

### Passage 34.10
## 10. Practical Applications & Unresolved Questions
- Forum selection is a strategic right of the maritime claimant; a defendant's "admiralty objection" to a lawsuit is meaningful only where admiralty jurisdiction elements are absent from the *facts*.
- Watch: *Lozman* "reasonable observer" cases (houseboats, barges); the LLA's survival after the 2024 *Raiders Retreat* choice-of-law harmonization; UNCLOS disputes in the South China Sea (non-party status limits U.S. standing to bring Part XV proceedings).

## [35] SPCU Volume IV: Separate Courts, Equity vs. Law & Judicial Jurisdiction (8 Passages)

### Passage 35.1
# VOLUME IV — SEPARATE COURTS AND JUDICIAL JURISDICTION

## 1. Executive Overview
The United States has many courts, but they all trace to identifiable constitutional or statutory authority, publish their decisions, and apply the Constitution. The architecture:

1. **Article III courts** (life-tenured judges): 94 district courts; 13 courts of appeals (12 regional + Federal Circuit); the Supreme Court.
2. **Article I legislative courts** (Congress creates under enumerated powers).
3. **Article IV territorial courts.**
4. **State courts** (sovereigns under their own constitutions).
5. **Tribal courts** (inherent sovereignty).
6. **Administrative adjudicators** (executive power).

The theory that any of these is a "secret" or "parallel" system without constitutional constraint has no support in any authority — and the doctrine of *strictly limited* subject-matter jurisdiction is the opposite of secret: it is enforced by courts on their own motion.

## 2. Article III Courts
Created under Art. III (life tenure, salary protection — *Marbury v. Madison*, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803)); *Martin v. Hunter's Lessee*, 14 U.S. (1 Wheat.) 304 (1816) (federal appellate power over state courts). Jurisdiction is statutory today: federal question (28 U.S.C. § 1331), diversity (§ 1332, > $75,000, *Strawbridge v. Curtiss*, 7 U.S. (3 Cranch) 267 (1806) complete diversity), admiralty (§ 1333), plus specialty grants.

### Passage 35.2
## 3. Article I Legislative Courts — BINDING
- *American Insurance Co. v. Canter*, 26 U.S. (1 Pet.) 511 (1828): Congress may create territorial courts with non-Article III judges.
- *Ex parte Bakelite Corp.*, 279 U.S. 438 (1929): categories of public-right disputes may go to legislative courts.
- *Palmore v. United States*, 411 U.S. 389 (1973): D.C. local courts are constitutional.
- **Bankruptcy courts:** *Northern Pipeline Constr. Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co.*, 458 U.S. 50 (1982) (Art. I bankruptcy judges cannot exercise ordinary Art. III jurisdiction over common-law suits); *Stern v. Marshall*, 564 U.S. 462 (2011); *Wellness Int'l Network v. Sharif*, 575 U.S. 665 (2015) (party consent permits).
- **U.S. Tax Court:** *Freytag v. Commissioner*, 501 U.S. 868 (1991); *Kuretski v. Commissioner*, 575 U.S. 51 (2015).
- **Military:** *Ex parte Milligan*, 71 U.S. (4 Wall.) 2 (1866); *Solorio v. United States*, 483 U.S. 435 (1987); U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces.

### Passage 35.3
## 4. Administrative Tribunals After *Jarkesy* (2024)
**SEC v. Jarkesy**, 603 U.S. 109 (U.S. June 27, 2024): when the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud (common-law analog), the **Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial in federal court**. Effect: in-house administrative penalty adjudication is unconstitutional for such claims; scope beyond securities fraud is being litigated (FTC, FINRA, etc.). *Loper Bright* (June 28, 2024) simultaneously restored judicial independence on statutory meaning. Administrative adjudication of genuinely "public rights" (taxes, benefits, immigration) continues.

## 5. Tribal and Immigration Courts
- **Tribal courts:** *United States v. Wheeler*, 435 U.S. 313 (1978) (retained sovereignty); *Duro*, *Lara*, *McGirt* (2020), *Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta* (2022), *Haaland v. Brackeen* (2023) — see Volume I § 2.6.
- **Immigration courts** (EOIR, Dept. of Justice): executive adjudicators; IJ decisions subject to BIA review then courts of appeals (8 U.S.C. § 1252). Status: constitutional as exercises of executive power over removable aliens.

### Passage 35.4
## 6. The Merger of Law and Equity
- FRCP Rule 2 (1938): "There is one form of action — the civil action."
- *Beacon Theatres, Inc. v. Westover*, 359 U.S. 500 (1959); *Dairy Queen, Inc. v. Wood*, 369 U.S. 469 (1962): legal issues get jury trial first.
- *Curtis v. Loether*, 415 U.S. 189 (1974): damages actions trigger the Seventh Amendment; *Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg*, 492 U.S. 33 (1989).
- **Consequence for pseudolaw:** the "law courts vs. equity courts" dichotomy no longer describes procedure; separate courts of chancery survive only in a few state names (e.g., Delaware Chancery — a specialized court, not a parallel system).

## 8. Personal Jurisdiction — Current Law
*International Shoe Co. v. Washington*, 326 U.S. 310 (1945) (minimum contacts); *Daimler AG v. Bauman*, 571 U.S. 117 (2014) (no general jurisdiction where neither incorporated nor principal place of business); *Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court*, 582 U.S. 255 (2017); *Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial Dist. Court*, 592 U.S. 351 (2021); **Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Ry. Co.**, 600 U.S. 122 (2023) — consent-by-registration: a company registering to do business in a state consents to suit there, and (per the controlling opinion) that consent satisfies due process.

## 9. How Jurisdiction Is Lawfully Challenged — and What Fails
**Succeeds (BINDING procedure):** Rule 12(b) motions; Rule 12(h)(3) dismissal for want of subject-matter jurisdiction at any time; removal/remand under 28 U.S.C. § 1447; abstention doctrines (*Younger v. Harris*, 401 U.S. 37 (1971); *Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp.*, 544 U.S. 280 (2005) (narrowing Rooker-Feldman)); Eleventh Amendment immunity; FSIA immunity.
**Fails uniformly (see Vol. VIII):** "I do not consent," "the flag has fringe," "I am a living man," "the court is a corporation," "admiralty jurisdiction over the land."

## [36] SPCU Volume V: Legal Personhood, Citizenship & Political Status (7 Passages)

### Passage 36.1
# VOLUME V — LEGAL PERSONHOOD, CITIZENSHIP, AND POLITICAL STATUS

## 1. Executive Overview
American law recognizes **persons** — natural and artificial — and attaches rights and duties to status (citizenship, nationality, domicile). It recognizes no third category of person (no "strawman," no "flesh-and-blood human" distinct from the "legal person"), and no political status a person can declare that exempts them from law. Every component of this volume is BINDING as of November 18, 2026, including *Trump v. Barbara* (U.S. June 30, 2026), which reaffirmed birthright citizenship.

### Passage 36.2
## 2. Natural and Legal Persons
- **1 U.S.C. § 1**: in federal statutes, "person" and "whoever" "include corporations, companies, associations, firms, partnerships, societies, and joint stock companies, as well as individuals." The statutory word *includes* ordinary human beings; it does not exclude them.
- **Corporate personhood:** *Trustees of Dartmouth College v. Woodward*, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 518 (1819) (charter as contract); *Pembina Consol. Silver Mining Co. v. Pennsylvania*, 125 U.S. 181 (1888); *Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific R.R.*, 118 U.S. 394 (1886) (equal-protection application via headnote — historically contested); *First National Bank v. Bellotti*, 435 U.S. 765 (1978); *Citizens United v. FEC*, 558 U.S. 310 (2010); *Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores*, 573 U.S. 682 (2014).
- **Key point:** treating a corporation as a "person" *adds* obligations and protections; it never subtracts them from humans. The human being in the courtroom IS the "person" the statute names. *United States v. Benabe*, 633 F.3d 581, 587 (7th Cir. 2011): whatever one's claimed status — "'sovereign citizen,' 'secured-party creditor,' or 'flesh-and-blood human being'" — one remains a person subject to law.

### Passage 36.3
## 3. Birth Registration — What the Documents Are
- Birth certificates are **state vital-records documents** (state vital statistics acts; model Uniform Vital Records Act). They establish identity and citizenship facts.
- There is **no federal "birth bond," no Treasury account, no CUSIP-numbered security** tied to a birth certificate. **TreasuryDirect's official fraud advisory** states plainly: [Birth Certificate Bonds — "This redemption scheme is a fraud"](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/laws-and-regulations/fraud/birth-certificate-bonds/). The Social Security Administration similarly warns against "birth certificate bond" and related claims.
- **Status: REJECTED/UNSUPPORTED** — and actively prosecuted when used (18 U.S.C. §§ 891–896, false liens; 26 U.S.C. § 6702, frivolous submissions).

### Passage 36.4
## 4. Citizenship — Current, Controlling Law
- **Birthright citizenship (jus soli):** *United States v. Wong Kim Ark*, 169 U.S. 649 (1898) — the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause makes citizens of all persons born in the United States (subject to limited exceptions: children of foreign diplomats, hostile occupiers, and historically, tribes).
- **2025–2026 litigation (verified this session):** Executive Order 14160 (Jan. 20, 2025) directed agencies to deny citizenship to certain U.S.-born children. *Trump v. CASA, Inc.*, 604 U.S. ___ (June 27, 2025), first curtailed the universal injunctions issued against the Order — without reaching the merits. Then, on **June 30, 2026, in *Trump v. Barbara*, No. 25-365, the Supreme Court struck the Order down as facially unconstitutional**, holding the Citizenship Clause means what *Wong Kim Ark* said it means. ([Opinion PDF](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-365_4hdj.pdf); [SCOTUSblog](https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/06/supreme-court-strikes-down-trumps-order-ending-birthright-citizenship/).)
- **Statutory citizenship:** 8 U.S.C. § 1401 (birth and derivation); § 1421 (naturalization); Indian Citizenship Act of 1924.
- **Slaughter-House Cases**, 83 U.S. (16 Wall.) 36 (1873): dual character of state and national citizenship.
- **Expatriation:** *Afroyim v. Rusk*, 387 U.S. 253 (1967) — citizenship cannot be lost absent voluntary relinquishment; *Vance v. Terrazas*, 444 U.S

### Passage 36.5
tate and national citizenship.
- **Expatriation:** *Afroyim v. Rusk*, 387 U.S. 253 (1967) — citizenship cannot be lost absent voluntary relinquishment; *Vance v. Terrazas*, 444 U.S. 252 (1980); 8 U.S.C. § 1481 (voluntary procedures).
- **Dual nationality:** *Kawakita v. United States*, 343 U.S. 717 (1952); *Mandoli v. Acheson*, 344 U.S. 133 (1952) — dual citizenship is permissible; allegiance problems attach to conduct, not status.
- **Passports:** *Haig v. Agee*, 453 U.S. 280 (1981).

### Passage 36.6
## 5. Domicile vs. Residence vs. "Political Status"
| Concept | Legal definition | Legal function |
|---|---|---|
| Citizenship | Nationality under 8 U.S.C. § 1401 or naturalization | Jurisdiction, voting, consular protection |
| Domicile | One's single true, fixed, permanent home (Restatement (Second) Conflicts §§ 11–23) | Diversity jurisdiction; probate; taxation |
| Residence | Physical presence, even extended | Some statutory benefits; tax contact |
| "Declared" status (e.g., "state citizen only," "Moorish national," "sovereign") | **No legal effect** | Rejected in every reported instance (Vol. VIII) |

"State citizen" theories (the *Zuber*/"original 1787 citizenship" line) were rejected in *Meads v. Meads*, 848 F.2d 66 (9th Cir. 1988), and countless successors; Moorish-national claims were rejected in, e.g., *United States v. Willis* (8th Cir. 2024) (collecting "repeatedly rejected" sovereign-Moorish tax claims).

## 6. Practical Applications
- Real changes of status are **statutory acts**: naturalization, renunciation before a consular officer (8 U.S.C. § 1481), expatriation filings. Declarations in court filings accomplish nothing except, sometimes, sanctions.
- Estate planning note (this agent's home discipline): status matters for situs, domicile, and treaty tie-breakers in cross-border estates — handled by instrument and evidence, never by "declaration."

### Passage 36.7
## 7. Unresolved Questions
- Children born abroad to mixed-status parents (8 U.S.C. § 1409 legitimacy rules) remain a patchwork.
- Residual challenges to *Trump v. Barbara* enforcement mechanics (30-day implementation window noted by commentators).

### Passage 37.1
# VOLUME VI — HISTORICAL STATUTES, TREATIES, AND FOUNDING DOCUMENTS
### With corrections of the popular misreadings of each (Directive 7)

## 1. Executive Overview
This volume states what each instrument **actually did**, and separates the historical record from interpretations that circulate online but have no support in the documents or the case law. The recurring pattern: real statutes are assigned imaginary powers (the Act of 1871, the Federal Reserve Act, H.J.Res. 192 of 1933), which courts have uniformly rejected.

## 2. Chronological Timeline — What Changed and What Did Not

It created ordinary federal courts; it did not create any "special" private system |

### Passage 37.5
### 2.4 The Act of 1871 — the real story
**Act of February 21, 1871, ch. 62, 16 Stat. 419 (An Act to provide a Government for the District of Columbia).** It consolidated the city of Washington, Georgetown, and Washington County into a single municipal government for the District, exercised under Congress's Article I § 8 cl. 17 power. It was a local reorganization. Congress replaced that form of government in 1874 and established a three-commissioner government in 1878; full local home rule came only with the **District of Columbia Self-Government and Governmental Reorganization Act of 1973**, Pub. L. 93-198 (D.C. Code § 1-201 et seq.).
**What it did NOT do:** create "a second Constitution," incorporate the United States as a private corporation, or suspend anything. *Palmore v. United States*, 411 U.S. 389 (1973), confirms D.C. local courts are valid Article I courts; *District of Columbia v. Heller*, 554 U.S. 570 (2008), applies the Constitution to D.C. without hesitation. PolitiFact (Feb. 2024) and USA Today (Mar. 2023) both fact-checked the "1871 corporation" claim and found no support; the "federal corporation" phrase that fuels the theory is 28 U.S.C. § 3002(15), a *definition for a government debt set-off chapter* — Volume VII dissects it.

### 2.6 1933 — the real joint resolution and the myth built on it
**H.J.Res. 192 (June 5, 1933), 48 Stat. 112** and the Gold Reserve Act of 1934: suspended the gold standard domestically, made gold-clause contracts unenforceable, and required gold coin/bullion delivery. It did **not** promise to discharge anyone's debts, create a "secret Treasury account," or authorize any individual to redeem anything. The "HJR 192 discharge" and " Accepted for Value" schemes built on it have been rejected every time they reach a court (Volume VIII). *United States v. Rickman*, 638 F.2d 182 (10th Cir. 1980), is representative: post-1933 paper-currency and gold-clause defenses to payment obligations are frivolous.

## [38] SPCU Volume VII: Commercial Law, UCC Articles 1-9, Express Trusts & Entities (6 Passages)

### Passage 38.1
# VOLUME VII — COMMERCIAL LAW, UCC, TRUSTS, AND GOVERNMENT ENTITIES

## 1. Executive Overview
This volume states what the Uniform Commercial Code actually does, what trusts actually are, what government corporations actually are — and dismantles the pseudo-uses of each. This is also the volume closest to this counsel's home discipline (trusts and estates), so its corrections are made with the same care a fiduciary would demand.

### Passage 38.2
## 2. The UCC — Actual Structure
- A **model code** drafted by ALI/ULC (first promulgated 1952; Article 9 revised 1998), adopted by all 50 states, D.C., and the territories. It governs **private commercial transactions**: sales (Art. 2), negotiable instruments (Art. 3), bank deposits (Art. 4), funds transfers (Art. 4A), letters of credit (Art. 5), bulk sales (Art. 6), documents of title (Art. 7), investment securities (Art. 8), **secured transactions (Art. 9)**.
- **Article 9 mechanics:** a security interest is created by *agreement* between debtor and secured party (§ 9-203) plus value and attachment. A **UCC-1 financing statement** (§ 9-502) merely *perfects* an interest that must already exist; filing offices index by debtor name. A filing creates nothing by itself.
- **The pseudo-theory:** that a person can file a UCC-1 against the "strawman," the government, or a creditor and thereby perfect a claim to Treasury accounts or discharge debts. **Status: REJECTED** in every reported instance; filings without an underlying obligation can constitute criminal false-lien conduct (18 U.S.C. §§ 891–896; see Vol. VIII).

### Passage 38.3
## 3. "Accepted for Value" (A4V) and Instrument Theories
- A4V claims that endorsing "Accepted for Value, Exemption No. ..." on a bill converts it into a Treasury discharge. **No provision of the UCC, the fiscal statutes, or 31 U.S.C. creates any such mechanism.** Courts treat A4V defenses as frivolous; taxpayers asserting them face 26 U.S.C. § 6702 penalties ($5,000 per frivolous submission) and § 6673 damages.
- The scheme's genealogy is verified: the "redemption"/A4V movement traces to Roger Elvick in the 1980s (SPLC profile; a Fourth Circuit opinion documents its Posse Comitatus origins); Elvick was among defendants in *United States v. Lorenzo*, 995 F.2d 1448 (5th Cir. 1993), a federal prosecution arising from fictitious commercial-paper schemes.

## 4. Trusts — the Real Law (and the Fake Kind)
**A valid express trust** requires: (1) a settlor with capacity, (2) intent, (3) ascertainable beneficiaries, (4) trust property, (5) a valid purpose (UTC § 402; Restatement (Third) of Trusts § 46). Trusts are **tax-neutral or tax-transparent** entities governed by Subchapter J (26 U.S.C. §§ 641–692) and the grantor-trust rules (§§ 671–679).

### Passage 38.4
**Abusive "patriot"/"pure"/"constitutional trust" schemes** — marketed as freeing property from taxation or judgment — have been rejected and penalized for decades:
- *Rodewald v. Commissioner*, 77 T.C. 490 (1981): substance over form — a trustee with no meaningful duties is a "goldfish bowl"; the settlor remains taxable owner.
- IRS "Abusive Trust Schemes" enforcement program; 26 U.S.C. § 6700 (promoter penalties); criminal convictions for trust-based tax evasion (e.g., *United States v. Anderson*, 444 F.3d 1155 (9th Cir. 2006), "Anderson's Ark" — verify before citing further).
- **Sovereign-trust myths:** no trust instrument can remove a person from the jurisdiction of the courts, create a "foreign status," or "capture" government accounts. The grantor-trust rules specifically *ignore* interposed entities when the grantor retains control (§§ 671–677) — the code anticipates and defeats these structures.

### Passage 38.5
## 5. Government Entities — the Real Definitions
- **Government corporations** exist by statute (31 U.S.C. § 9101 list: Amtrak, TVA, FDIC, U.S. Postal Service, etc.). A corporation-for-government-purpose is a creature of Congress — not evidence of a "corporate United States."
- **28 U.S.C. § 3002(15)** — the most misquoted definition in America. Text (LII-verified): for purposes of the set-off chapter (18→28 U.S.C. ch. 176 set-off provisions), "'United States' means — (A) a Federal corporation; (B) an agency, department, commission, board, or other entity of the United States; or (C) an instrumentality of the United States." It is a *catch-all definition ensuring the government can be reached in set-off proceedings* — a creditor-friendly, not status-defining, provision. PolitiFact (Feb. 2024) and USA Today (Mar. 2023) fact-checked the "U.S. is a private corporation" claim: **false**. Courts reject the argument wherever raised.
- **The Act of 1871** created a *municipal corporation for the District of Columbia* — a local government form. A municipal corporation is a common unit of local government; it is not a private company and says nothing about the national government's character. **Status of the "corporate U.S." theory: REJECTED/UNSUPPORTED.**

### Passage 38.6
## 6. Public Law vs. Private Law
A jurisprudential distinction (public law = state's relations with persons; private law = persons' relations with each other) — with a modern procedural meaning: **"Public Law" is the standard designation of every federal session law** (e.g., Pub. L. No. 93-198). The pseudolegal claim that "public law" statutes bind only government or that "private law" secretly governs citizens is **UNSUPPORTED**.

## 7. What Legitimate Commercial Law Offers
- Real secured transactions (UCC-9), real negotiable-instrument defenses (UCC-3), real trusts, real consumer-protection claims (FDCPA 15 U.S.C. § 1692; FCRA), and real bankruptcy relief (11 U.S.C.). These are the lawful paths to debt problems — the redemption toolkit is a path to sanctions and prison.

## 8. Source Notes

## [39] SPCU Volume VIII: Verified Constitutional & Trust Law vs. Rejected Pseudolaw Guardrails (9 Passages)

### Passage 39.1
# VOLUME VIII — CONTROVERSIAL SOVEREIGNTY THEORIES AND JUDICIAL VERIFICATION
### Directive 4 + Directive 8 applied: every proposition stated, traced, and classified

## 1. Executive Overview
This volume applies the six-stage verification protocol (assert → supporting authority → contrary authority → classify → verify → practical consequences) to the principal pseudolegal theories. **The finding, uniform across five decades of litigation and confirmed by the verified research this session: none of these propositions has ever been sustained by any U.S. court.** A 2023 review of 530 U.S. sovereign-citizen judgments found the Strawman theory "universally rejected" (CanLII commentary); Canadian authority *Meads v. Meads*, 2012 ABQB 571 (Alta. Q.B., Rooke ACJ), coined the umbrella term **"Organized Pseudolegal Commercial Arguments" (OPCA)** for the same phenomena.

**Standing caution:** courts sanction these arguments (28 U.S.C. § 1927; FRCP 11; inherent power — *United States v. Ferguson*, 540 F. Supp. 2d 1275 (N.D. Okla. 2008) ($10,000 plus mandatory essays)); filing bogus liens is a federal crime (18 U.S.C. §§ 891–896); the FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin identifies sovereign-citizen violence and "paper terrorism" as a persistent domestic threat.

### Passage 39.5
## 3. Deep Dives on the Four Most Litigated Theories

### 3.1 The sovereign citizen / "individual sovereignty" cluster
**Claim:** a person may renounce implied federal obligations while retaining U.S. protection, often framed as "14th Amendment citizen" vs. "state citizen."
**Contrary authority (verified):** *Meads v. Meads*, 848 F.2d 66 (9th Cir. 1988) — the canonical American catalogue of "positivist/sovereign" arguments and their variants ("freemen," "constitutionalists," "Posse Comitatus"), all rejected; *Benabe*, 633 F.3d 581, 587 (7th Cir. 2011) — "[r]egardless of an individual's claimed status ... he is still a person subject to the revenue laws," sovereign-citizen immunity defenses "frivolous"; 8th Cir. (2024) — repeat sovereign filings forfeit appeal considerations.
**Practical consequence:** dismissal; sanctions; loss of appeals; state vexatious-litigant orders; in extreme cases criminal prosecution for paper terrorism.

### Passage 39.6
### 3.2 The strawman / redemption complex
**Claim:** the government created a secret "strawman" (the ALL-CAPS name) holding an exemption account; A4V endorsements and UCC-1 filings can tap it.
**Origins (verified):** Roger Elvick, 1980s; SPLC and judicial opinions trace the lineage through Posse Comitatus circles; *United States v. Lorenzo*, 995 F.2d 1448 (5th Cir. 1993) — federal prosecutions of fictitious-obligation schemes in which Elvick was a defendant.
**Contrary authority:** TreasuryDirect: birth-certificate bonds "do not exist" and related schemes are fraud; the 530-judgment review (2023): universal rejection; criminal statutes: 18 U.S.C. § 514 (fictitious obligations), § 152, §§ 891–896 (false liens), 26 U.S.C. § 7206.
**Practical consequence:** a documented fraud economy — promoters sell templates; users absorb liability.

### Passage 39.7
### 3.3 The admiralty/courtroom-ritual cluster
**Claim:** flags, the judge's presence/absence, the "star spangled banner" oath rituals, or the courtroom's geography invoke admiralty or ecclesiastical jurisdiction and void proceedings.
**Contrary authority (verified):** *McCann v. Greenway*, 952 F. Supp. 647 (W.D. Mo. 1997) (gold-fringe theory frivolous); broader pattern confirmed by legal scholarship (Montana Law Review 2019, Kalinowski) and fact-checks (Lead Stories 2021). Jurisdiction is determined by facts and statute, never by drapery.
**Why the theory persists:** it converts the observed (flags in every courtroom — required by 4 U.S.C. § 5 display conventions and VA/custom rules) into the imagined (a hidden jurisdiction).

### 3.4 Comparative pseudolaw (for completeness)
Canada: *Meads v. Meads*, 2012 ABQB 571 — the OPCA taxonomy ("double Republic," "Freeman-on-the-Land," "paper terrorist"), adopted across Commonwealth courts; UK: "Freeman" arguments rejected (*R v. Imperial? *— represented in NSW Judicial Commission bench book, "Sovereign citizens: ideology, impacts and judicial responses," 2023); the movement has spread to 26+ countries (Lowy Institute analysis, 2024).

### Passage 39.8
## 4. What Courts Actually Offer (the legitimate toolkit)
Real jurisdictional challenges (Rule 12), real constitutional litigation, real tax controversy procedure (26 U.S.C. §§ 6212–6213), real debt relief (bankruptcy), real consumer defenses (FDCPA). Every objective pseudolaw promises is achievable by lawful means; every pseudolaw vehicle is a sanctioned dead end.

## [40] SPCU Volume IX: Jurisdictional Challenges, Administrative Record & Procedural Law (4 Passages)

### Passage 40.1
# VOLUME IX — JURISDICTIONAL CHALLENGES AND PROCEDURAL LAW

## 1. Executive Overview
Jurisdiction is the court's lawful power to act; procedure is how it is tested. The rules are mechanical, strict, and mostly unforgiving of delay — and they are entirely different from the pseudolegal "non-consent" fantasy. This volume is the procedural field manual for Volume IV.

## 2. Never Waivable vs. Waivable
| Rule | Subject-matter jurisdiction | Personal jurisdiction | Venue | Immunities |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Can be raised anytime? | Yes — court *must* dismiss, even on appeal (FRCP 12(h)(3)) | No — waived if not timely raised | No — forfeiture (28 U.S.C. § 1406; *Moore v. Beaulieu*? — general rule) | Yes/No by type (Eleventh Amendment: structural; FSIA: must be raised or forfeited? — courts split pre-*Vitol*) |
| Key authority | *Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp.*, 546 U.S. 500 (2006); *Henderson v. Shinseki*, 562 U.S. 428 (2011) | *Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites*, 456 U.S. 694 (1982) (waiver as consent) | FRCP 12(b)(3) | *Vitol, S.A. v. Primerose Shipping*, 708 F.3d 527 (4th Cir. 2013) (FSIA forfeiture) |

**Note on FSIA:** sovereign immunity "is not a mere procedural rule" — it strips jurisdiction (Kuwait Airways v. American Sec. Bank, 590 F.2d 1270 (D.C. Cir. 1978)).

### Passage 40.2
## 3. The Lawful Challenge Sequence
1. **Answer or Rule 12 motion deadline** (21 days after service; waivable).
2. **Rule 12(b) defenses:** (1) lack of SMJ; (2) lack of PJ; (3) improper venue; (4) insufficient process; (5) insufficient service; (6) failure to state a claim; (7) failure to join a Rule 19 party.
3. **Removal/remand:** 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1453; § 1447(c) 30-day remand clock for defects other than SMJ.
4. **Appeal:** final-judgment rule (28 U.S.C. § 1291); collateral-order doctrine (*Cohen v. Beneficial Indus. Loan Corp.*, 337 U.S. 541 (1949)).
5. **Supreme Court:** certiorari (28 U.S.C. § 1257) — discretionary.

## 4. Abstention and Restraint Doctrines
*Younger v. Harris*, 401 U.S. 37 (1971) (federal courts decline to enjoin pending state proceedings); *Pullman* (certification of state-law questions); *Burford* (complex state regulatory schemes); *Colorado River* (concurrent proceedings); *Rooker-Feldman*, as narrowed by *Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp.*, 544 U.S. 280 (2005) — lower federal courts cannot review final state-court judgments; only the Supreme Court can.

### Passage 40.3
## 5. Sanctions — the Real Enforcement Regime
| Authority | Trigger | Exposure |
|---|---|---|
| FRCP 11 | Frivolous or bad-faith filings | Money, nonmonetary sanctions |
| 28 U.S.C. § 1927 | Bad-faith multiplication of proceedings | Attorney's fees |
| Inherent power | *Chambers v. NASCO, Inc.*, 501 U.S. 32 (1991) | Any appropriate sanction |
| 26 U.S.C. § 6702 / § 6673 | Frivolous tax submissions/positions | $5,000 per submission; damages up to $25,000 |
| 18 U.S.C. §§ 891–896 | False liens against federal officers | Criminal (fines, imprisonment) |
| 18 U.S.C. § 514 | Fictitious obligations | Criminal |
| Vexatious-litigant orders | *Safir v. U.S. Lines*, 79 F.3d 1526 (2d Cir. 1996) (en banc) | Prefiling review |
| 28 U.S.C. § 1915(g) | Three strikes (prisoner filings) | Filing-bar |

**Verified example:** *United States v. Ferguson*, 540 F. Supp. 2d 1275 (N.D. Okla. 2008) — $10,000 sanction plus a mandatory-essay order against a litigant whose filings "advocate ... a non-existent 'sovereign' status."

### Passage 40.4
## 6. Practical Checklist — A Jurisdictional Challenge That Will Actually Work
1. Identify the grant of jurisdiction (statute + article).
2. Test the *elements* (maritime facts? diversity complete? amount? well-pleaded complaint?).
3. Preserve personal/venue objections in the first responsive pleading.
4. Raise immunity (Eleventh Amendment, FSIA, tribal) early — correctly, by party and remedy type.
5. Never couple a valid challenge with pseudolegal declarations — they contaminate the record and invite sanctions.

## 7. Unresolved Questions
- Forfeiture of FSIA immunity when raised late (circuit variation).
- *Mallory* consent-by-registration boundaries.
- Post-*Jarkesy* scope of administrative penalty adjudication.
